Block A is released from rest from a position where the string is horizontal. Let V be the horizontal velocity of the track and vrel be the velocity of block B relative to the track at the highest point of the loop. At this point, the velocity of B in the ground frame is (V – vrel) horizontally. questions.text: Two particles B and C of masses m and 2m respectively are connected by a light ideal spring of natural length L and spring constant k. They are initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface with the spring relaxed. A third particle A of mass m moves on the surface with speed v0 in a direction perpendicular to the spring. Particle A strikes and sticks to particle B. In the subsequent motion, the maximum extension of the spring is observed to be L/2. What is the value of the spring constant k?

By conservation of linear momentum, the combined mass AB(mass mAB = 2m) acquires a velocity v1 = \(\frac{mv0}{m+m}\) = \(\frac{v0}{2}\) in a direction perpendicular to the spring. The velocity of the center of mass (COM) of the AB − Csystem is Vcm = \(\frac{mABv1+mC(0)}{mAB+mC}\) = \(\frac{2m(v0/2)}{4m}\) = \(\frac{v0}{4}\), directed parallel to the initial velocity of A. We analyze the subsequent motion in the COM frame. The initial velocities in this frame are uAB = \(\frac{v0}{2}\) − \(\frac{v0}{4}\) = \(\frac{v0}{4}\) and uC = 0 − \(\frac{v0}{4}\) = − \(\frac{v0}{4}\). Both velocities are perpendicular to the spring. The reduced mass of the system is μ = \(\frac{(2m)(2m)}{2m+2m}\) = m. The initial kinetic energy in the COM frame is Kcm = \(\frac{1}{2}\) \(μv_{rel}^{2}\) = \(\frac{1}{2}\) m( \(\frac{v0}{2}\) \()^{2}\) = \(\frac{mv_{0}^{2}}{8}\). Since no external torques act on the system about its COM, Lcmis conserved. At the maximum extension xm = L/2, the radial velocity of the masses in the COM frame is zero. The distance between ABand Cis r = L + \(\frac{L}{2}\) = \(\frac{3L}{2}\). By conservation of mechanical energy in the COM frame, Kcm = Krot + Uspring. questions.text: A particle P is initially at rest at the very top of a smooth hemispherical surface of radius R, which is fixed on a horizontal plane. The particle is then given an initial horizontal velocity v0. Which of the following statements is INCORRECT?
options: If v0 = \(\frac{−−−−}{√gR/2}\), the particle leaves the sphere when it has fallen a vertical distance of R/6.
If magnitude of v0 is just greater than zero, the particle leaves the surface at a height of R/3 from the horizontal plane.
The minimum value of v0 for the particle to leave the sphere immediately is \(√gR^{−−−}.\)
If the particle leaves the surface after falling a distance R/3, then its initial velocity was just greater than zero.
questions.solution: By conservation of energy, \(v^{2}\) = \(v_{0}^{2}\) + 2gR (1 − cos θ). The particle leaves the surface when the normal force is zero, meaning mgcos θ = \(\frac{mv^{2}}{R}\). This yields 3gRcos θ = v20 + 2gR. If v0 = 0, cos θ = \(\frac{2}{3}\). The height of the particle from the ground (the horizontal plane) at this moment is h = Rcos θ = \(\frac{2R}{3}\), making statement B incorrect as it states a height of R/3.

questions.text: A particle of mass m is constrained to move along the positive x-axis under the influence of a conservative force field. The potential energy of the particle is given by U (x) = \(\frac{a}{x^{2}}\) − \(\frac{b}{x}\), where a and b are positive constants. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
options: If the particle is released from rest at x = \(\frac{3a}{2b}\), it will perform oscillatory motion and its maximum distance from the origin will be \(\frac{3a}{b}\).
If the particle is projected from the equilibrium position, the minimum kinetic energy required for it to escape to infinity is \(\frac{b^{2}}{2a}\).
The particle has a stable equilibrium position at x = \(\frac{2a}{b}\), where its potential energy is − \(\frac{b^{2}}{4a}\).
If the particle is released from rest at x = a, b its maximum kinetic energy during the subsequent motion will be \(\frac{b^{2}}{4a}\).
questions.solution: The force on the particle is F = − \(\frac{dU}{dx}\) = \(\frac{2a}{x^{3}}\) − \(\frac{b}{x^{2}}\). Equilibrium occurs where the net force is zero, which yields x = \(\frac{2a}{b}\). To check stability, we evaluate the second derivative of the potential energy: U ′′ (x) = \(\frac{6a}{x^{4}}\) − \(\frac{2b}{x^{3}}\). At x = \(\frac{2a}{b}\), U ′′ ( \(\frac{2a}{b}\) ) = \(\frac{6a}{(16a^{4} /b^{4} )}\) − \(\frac{2b}{(8a^{3} /b^{3} )}\) = \(\frac{3b^{4}}{8a^{3}}\) − \(\frac{2b^{4}}{8a^{3}}\) = \(\frac{b^{4}}{8a^{3}}\) > 0, confirming it is a stable equilibrium. The potential energy at this point is Umin = \(\frac{a}{(2a/b)^{2}}\) − \(\frac{b}{(2a/b)}\) = − \(\frac{b^{2}}{4a}\). Option C is correct. If the particle is released from rest at x = a, its b initial kinetic energy is zero, so its total mechanical energy is E = U ( \(\frac{a}{b}\) ) = \(\frac{a}{(a/b)^{2}}\) − \(\frac{b}{(a/b)}\) = \(\frac{b^{2}}{a}\) − \(\frac{b^{2}}{a}\) = 0. By conservation of mechanical energy, K (x) = E − U (x) = −U (x). The maximum kinetic energy occurs where U (x) is minimum, so Kmax = −Umin = − (− \(\frac{b^{2}}{4a}\) ) = \(\frac{b^{2}}{4a}\). Option D is correct. If released from rest at x = 3a, the total energy 2b is E = U ( \(\frac{3a}{2b}\) ) = \(\frac{a}{(9a^{2} /4b^{2} )}\) − \(\frac{b}{(3a/2b)}\) = \(\frac{4b^{2}}{9a}\) − \(\frac{2b^{2}}{3a}\) = − \(\frac{2b^{2}}{9a}\). Since E < 0, the motion is bounded and oscillatory. The turning points of the motion are found by setting U (x) = E: \(\frac{a}{x^{2}}\) − \(\frac{b}{x}\) = − \(\frac{2b^{2}}{9a}\). Multiplying the entire equation by \(9ax^{2}\)gives \(9a^{2}\) − 9abx = \(−2b^{2} x^{2}\), which rearranges to the quadratic equation \(2b^{2} x^{2}\) − 9abx + \(9a^{2}\) = 0. Factoring this yields (2bx − 3a) (bx − 3a) = 0. The roots are x = \(\frac{3a}{2b}\) (the release point) and x = \(\frac{3a}{b}\) (the maximum distance from the origin). Option A is correct. For the particle to escape to infinity, its total mechanical energy must be E ≥ 0. If projected from the equilibrium position, E = K + Umin = K − \(\frac{b^{2}}{4a}\) ≥ 0. The minimum kinetic energy required to escape is therefore K = \(\frac{b^{2}}{4a}\). Option B claims it is \(\frac{b^{2}}{2a}\), so it is incorrect.

By the Work-Energy Theorem, the work done by the impulse equals the change in kinetic energy: W = Kf − Ki = \(\frac{1}{2}\) m\(u^{2}\) − \(\frac{1}{2}\) m\(v_{0}^{2}\) = 2mgL − 3 mgL = 5 mgL 4 4 Thus, Option A is correct. with Evaluate the magnitude and direction of the impulse. The impulse is \(\vec{J}\) = \(m \vec{u}\) − \(m \vec{v} 0\) = m (±\(√gL^{−−} \hat{i}\) − \(−_{√}−_{1.5gL}−−−_{\hat{j}}\) ± \(ˆ_{√3gLk}^{−−−}\)). questions.text: A small ball of mass m is suspended from the end A of an L-shaped massless rigid frame fixed to a block of mass 2m. The block is placed on a smooth horizontal table. The ball is given a horizontal impulse so as to impart it a velocity of u. The ball begins to rotate in a circle of radius R about the point A, while the block and frame slide on the table. The rod does not interfere with the string during the motion. The tension in the string at the instant the ball is at the topmost position is \(\frac{mu^{2}}{R}\) − xmg. Find the value of x. (Assume that u is sufficiently large to reach the top most position)
questions.solution: Working in the Center of Mass (CM) frame, the reduced mass is μ = \(\frac{m(2m)}{3m}\) = \(\frac{2}{3}\) m. The initial kinetic energy in the CM frame is Kcm = \(\frac{1}{2}\) \(μu^{2}\) = \(\frac{1}{3}\) \(mu^{2}\). At the top, the ball gains potential energy ΔU = 2mgR. By conservation of energy, \(K_{cm}^{'}\) = Kcm − ΔU, so \(\frac{1}{3}\) m\(v_{rel}^{2}\) = \(\frac{1}{3}\) m\(u^{2}\) − 2mgR ⇒ \(v_{rel}^{2}\) = \(u^{2}\) − 6gR. The tension at the top is T = \(\frac{mv_{rel}^{2}}{R}\) − mg = \(\frac{mu^{2} −6mgR}{R}\) − mg = \(\frac{mu^{2}}{R}\) − 7mg. Thus, x = 7.

questions.text:
A uniform object of outer radius R is initially made of a base material of uniform density ρ (mass per unit volume for a 3D object, mass per unit area for a 2D object). A cavity of radius R/2 is created in the object such that the centre of the cavity is at a distance of R/2 from the geometric centre of the object. This cavity is then completely filled with a new material of uniform density ρfill. Let dcm be the distance of the new centre of mass of the composite object from its geometric centre. List-I contains four cases of such objects. List-II contains five possible values for dcm. Each object in List-I matches exactly one value in List-II. Match the objects in List-I with their correct dcm in List-II.

List-IList-II
PA solid sphere with $\rho_{\text{fill}} = 3\rho$1$R/6$
QA circular disk with $\rho_{\text{fill}} = 3\rho$2$R/10$
RA solid sphere with $\rho_{\text{fill}} = \rho/2$3$R/14$

5$R/30$
questions.solution: The composite object can be modelled as the original uniform object of mass M0(with its centre of mass at the origin) plus an additional mass ΔM placed at the centre of the cavity, which is at x = R/2. The additional mass is due to the difference in density: ΔM = \((ρ_{fill}\) − ρ) Vc, where Vc is the volume (or area) of the cavity. The total mass of the composite object is Mtotal = M0 + ΔM. The new centre of mass is located at xcm = \(\frac{M0(0)+ΔM(R/2)}{M0+ΔM}\) = \(\frac{ΔM(R/2)}{M0+ΔM}\). The distance is dcm =∣ xcm∣. For a solid sphere (P), Vc = V0/8. With \(ρ_{fill}\) = 3ρ, ΔM = 2ρ (V0/8) = M0/4. Thus xcm = \(\frac{(M0/4)(R/2)}{M0+M0/4}\) = \(\frac{M0R/8}{5M0/4}\) = R/10. This matches (2). For a circular disk (Q), Vc = V0/4. With \(ρ_{fill}\) = 3ρ, ΔM = 2ρ (V0/4) = M0/2. Thus xcm = \(\frac{(M0/2)(R/2)}{M0+M0/2}\) = \(\frac{M0R/4}{3M0/2}\) = R/6. This matches (1). For a solid sphere (R), \(ρ_{fill}\) = ρ/2. ΔM = (ρ/2 − ρ) (V0/8) = −M0/16. Thus xcm = \(\frac{(−M0/16)(R/2)}{M0−M0/16}\) = \(\frac{−M0R/32}{15M0/16}\) = −R/30. The distance is dcm = R/30. This matches (5). questions.text: The potential energy U(x) of a particle of mass m = 1 kg moving along the x-axis under the action of a conservative force is shown in the figure. The graph consists of straight line segments joining the points (0, 10), (2, 2), (4, 8), (6, 0), (8, 12), and (10, 12), where x is in meters and U(x) is in Joules. The particle is subjected to four different initial conditions given in List-I. Match each case in List-I with the maximum kinetic energy acquired by the particle during its subsequent motion, given in List-II. Each List-I entry matches exactly one List-II entry.
questions.solution: The total mechanical energy E = K + U (x) of the particle is conserved. The particle can only move in regions where E ≥ U (x), turning around at points where E = U (x). The maximum kinetic energy is Kmax = E − Umin, where Umin is the absolute minimum of the potential energy within the particle's accessible region. For (P), the particle is released from rest at x = 1 m. From the graph, the segment from x = 0 to x = 2 is U (x) = 10 − 4x, so U (1) = 6 J. Thus, E = 6 J. The particle moves to the right (since the force F = −dU /dx = 4 N is positive). It passes the local minimum at x = 2 m(U = 2 J) and encounters the barrier at x = 4 m(U = 8 J). Since E = 6 J < 8 J, it cannot cross the barrier and turns around. The minimum potential energy in its accessible region is Umin = 2 J. Therefore, Kmax = 6 − 2 = 4 J. This matches (1). For (Q), the particle is released from rest at x = 7 m. The segment from x = 6 to x = 8 is U (x) = 6x − 36, so U (7) = 6 J. Thus, E = 6 J. The particle moves to the left, passes the absolute minimum at x = 6 m (U = 0 J), and encounters the barrier at x = 4 m(U = 8 J). Since E = 6 J < 8 J, it cannot cross the barrier. The minimum potential energy in its accessible region is Umin = 0 J. Therefore, Kmax = 6 − 0 = 6 J. This matches (2). For (R), the particle is projected from x = 3 m with K = 5 J. The segment from x = 2 to x = 4 is U (x) = 3x − 4, so U (3) = 5 J. Thus, E = 5 + 5 = 10 J. It moves to the right and encounters the barrier at x = 4 m ( U = 8 J). Since E = 10 J > 8 J, it crosses the barrier and enters the deeper potential well, reaching x = 6 m where U = 0 J. The minimum potential energy in its entire accessible region is Umin = 0 J. Therefore, Kmax = 10 − 0 = 10 J. This matches (5). For (S), the particle is projected from x = 3 m with K = 4 J in the negative x-direction. Thus, E = 5 + 4 = 9 J. It moves to the left, passes x = 2 m (U = 2 J), and turns around at x = 0.25 m where U = 9 J. It then moves to the right. When it reaches the barrier at x = 4 m, U (4) = 8 J. Since E = 9 J > 8 J, it crosses the barrier and reaches the deeper well at x = 6 m where U = 0 J. The minimum potential energy in its accessible region is Umin = 0 J. Therefore, Kmax = 9 − 0 = 9 J. This matches (4).

questions.text:
A person of mass m stands at the left end of a uniform boat of mass M and length L. The boat is initially at rest in still water. The person walks towards the right end with a constant speed u relative to the boat. Neglect water resistance. Match each entry in List-I with the correct entries in List-II. More than one option may be correct.

List-I
Physical quantity		List-II
Property
PDisplacement of the boat when the person reaches the other end1Magnitude is $\frac{mL}{M + m}$
QDisplacement of the person relative to the ground2Magnitude is $\frac{ML}{M + m}$
RVelocity of the boat while the person is walking3Directed towards the left
SVelocity of the person relative to the ground4Directed towards the right
5Magnitude is $\frac{mu}{M + m}$
6Magnitude is $\frac{Mu}{M + m}$
questions.solution: Take the rightward direction as positive. Since no external horizontal force acts on the person–boat system, the horizontal position of its centre of mass remains unchanged. Let xB be the displacement of the boat and xP the displacement of the person relative to the ground. Conservation of the centre-of-mass position gives mxP + M xB = 0. The person travels a distance Lrelative to the boat, so xP − xB = L. Solving, xB = − \(\frac{mL}{M+m}\), xP = \(\frac{ML}{M+m}\). Thus, the boat moves left by \(\frac{mL}{M+m}\), whereas the person moves right by \(\frac{ML}{M+m}\). Therefore, (P)→(1), (3), (Q)→(2), (4). While the person is walking, let vB and vP be the velocities of the boat and the person relative to the ground. Conservation of horizontal linear momentum gives mvP + M vB = 0. Since the person moves with speed u relative to the boat, vP − vB = u. Solving, vB = − \(\frac{mu}{M+m}\), vP = \(\frac{Mu}{M+m}\). Hence, the boat moves left with speed \(\frac{mu}{M+m}\), and the person moves right with speed \(\frac{Mu}{M+m}\). Therefore, (R) →(5), (3), (S)→(6), (4).

questions.text: In alkaline treatment of cyanide, the net redox change may be represented as \(CN^{–}\) + \(OCl^{–}\) → \(CNO^{–}\) + \(Cl^{–}\) Oxidation numbers are to be assigned by the usual electronegativity convention, while formal charges may differ among resonance contributors. Which statements are correct?
options: C changes from +2 in \(CN^{–}\) to +4 in \(CNO^{–}\); therefore the n-factor of cyanide for this change is 2.
The oxidation number of nitrogen changes from –3 to –1 because oxygen is inserted into the species.
Cl in \(OCl^{–}\) changes from +1 to –1, so one mole of hypochlorite is stoichiometrically required per mole of cyanide.

questions.solution: In cyanide, assigning bonding electrons to nitrogen gives carbon +2 and nitrogen −3. In cyanate, oxygen is −2 and nitrogen remains −3, forcing carbon to +4. Carbon therefore loses two electrons, while chlorine in hypochlorite gains two electrons; the balanced net equation has a 1:1 cyanide-to- hypochlorite ratio. Resonance redistributes formal charge but does not alter oxidation-number bookkeeping.

So, u + v = \(\frac{2b}{a}\) and uv = \(\frac{3c}{a}\). Since a, b, c are in A.P., c = 2b − a. Therefore, \(\frac{c}{a}\) = \(\frac{2b}{a}\) − 1 = u + v − 1. Hence, uv = 3 (u + v − 1). uv − 3u − 3v + 3 = 0, (u − 3) (v − 3) = 6. The absolute difference of the roots is 5, so |u − v| = 5. The only positive solution is {u, v} = {4, 9}. Therefore, the roots are −4, − 9. Thus statement (A) is true. Also, u + v = 13 = \(\frac{2b}{a}\), \(\frac{b}{a}\) = \(\frac{13}{2}\). Further, uv = 36 = \(\frac{3c}{a}\), so \(\frac{c}{a}\) = 12. questions.text: For real a, let f (x) = \(x^{2}\) + ax + 3 on the closed interval [–3, 5]. Count the values of a for which the maximum of f is 33 and, simultaneously, the minimum of f is attained at an interior point of the interval.
questions.solution: The function f (x) = \(x^{2}\) + ax + 3 is an upward-opening parabola. Therefore, its maximum on the closed interval [−3, 5] occurs at one of the endpoints. The endpoint values are f (−3) = 12 − 3a and f (5) = 28 + 5a. For the maximum to be 33, one endpoint value must equal 33, while the other must not exceed 33 First, 12 − 3a = 33 gives a = −7. For a = −7, f (5) = 28 − 35 = −7 < 33. The vertex is at x = − \(\frac{a}{2}\) = 72, which lies inside (−3, 5). Second, 28 + 5a = 33 gives a = 1. For a = 1, f (−3) = 9 < 33. The vertex is at x = − 12, which also lies inside (−3, 5). Thus there are two admissible values of a.
